For each of the cryogenic fuels discussed in this report, airport fueling installations and aircraft would need major adaptations, including vacuum-insulated storage tanks, cryogenic-rated transfer equipment, and strict safety protocols. Given the difference in thermophysical properties between cryogenic fuels and Jet A, creating standard procedures for handling and dispensing LH LNG, and/or LE at airports is paramount. These procedures must 2, be finalized before airport officials can plan and implement cryogenic infrastructure. Several companies have already begun developing aircraft technology with hydrogen fuel cell propulsion systems—specifically for personal aircraft and regional turbo-propeller airframes. Using LH for short-haul flights is more realistic given energy density limitations of the fuel. If 2 LH were to be used in longer-haul flights, it would require novel or modified airframes to 2 accommodate both storage tanks and seating capacity. The development of cryogenic aircraft technologies would encounter long lead times and require significant capital investment. The use of cryogenic hydrogen, stored as a liquid at −253°C (20 K), for air mobility applications requires significant development before it can compete in the aviation fuel market. At present, most hydrogen production and end uses are colocated to avoid the complex infrastructure and associated costs with transporting the molecule in a liquid or highly compressed state. The cost to deliver or produce it directly at an airport in a liquefied state can decline over time to become more competitive with alternatives, but this requires policy support and/or industry investment to spur technology maturation. With low airport LH demand levels (~10 metric tons per day or 2 less), liquid hydrogen trucking to an airport is the most viable delivery option. If airport demands scale beyond these levels, on-site liquid hydrogen production should be considered if the airport has space and electrical capacity to accommodate the new systems. LNG, which can be produced from abundant domestic natural gas or renewable natural gas (RNG) from the aerobic digestion or thermal gasification of wastes, was evaluated for aviation because of its relatively high specific energy, low cost, and less polluting combustion profile compared to Jet A.
